title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)

segments.voice: Yesterday in Sanskrit sounds for readers, the line over a letter: a long vowel, stay longer. Rāma, long then short. Did you slow down on one? Today the consonants, and a map of the mouth. Day one thousand forty-two.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THE LINE MEANS: STAY LONGER.`

segments.voice: A chakra, in a scholar's book, is spelled c, a, k, r, a. Cakra. A reader who has heard the word chakra all their life stops and frowns. Did someone drop a letter? No. In the careful system of spelling Sanskrit in English letters, c is always said ch, as in church. It looks like a typo until you know the map behind it. And the map behind it is worth having: the consonants laid out in rows, each row a place in your own mouth.
screen: `CAKRA, NOT A TYPO.` → `C IS ALWAYS CH.` → `A MAP OF THE MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the map. Say each sound slowly as it comes, and feel where it lands. The first row is made at the back, in the throat: ka, kha, ga, gha, and a nasal, nga. The second row moves forward to the palate, where the middle of the tongue rises: cha, chha, ja, jha, and nya. The third row is made with the tip of the tongue curled up to the roof of the mouth. We'll spend tomorrow on that one. The fourth row comes forward again, the tongue touching the teeth: ta, tha, da, dha, na. And the last row is made at the lips: pa, pha, ba, bha, ma. Throat, palate, roof, teeth, lips. Say the first sound of each row in order, ka, cha, ta, ta, pa, and the sound walks forward out of you, from the back of the mouth to the front. Every row ends the same way, with a sound that hums through the nose. And inside each row, plain sounds sit beside breathy ones, ka beside kha; that pattern gets its own day soon. The Upanishad's list for the teaching of sound starts with the letter, varna, and laid out this way the alphabet is more than a list to memorize. It's a description of the body speaking. For a reader, this map does real work. It explains why c is ch: it lives in the palate row. Cakra is chakra. Candra, the moon, is chandra. And it means that when you meet a strange spelling, you can ask one useful question: where in the mouth does this sound live? Find the place, and the sound usually follows.
screen: `THROAT: KA. PALATE: CHA.` · `ROOF, THEN TEETH: TA, TA.` · `LIPS: PA. EACH ROW ENDS IN A HUM.` · `C IS CH: CAKRA IS CHAKRA.` · then, large: `WHERE IN THE MOUTH DOES IT LIVE?`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, mouth relaxed. On one out-breath, say slowly: ka. Feel it at the back of the throat. Next breath: cha. Feel the middle of the tongue rise. Next: ta, with the tongue curled back. Next: ta, at the teeth. Next: pa, at the lips. Then rest for a breath, and walk the sounds forward again: ka, cha, ta, ta, pa. Go slowly enough to feel each place. Then end with the hum that closes the last row, softly, ma, at the lips, and let it fade into the breath. The bell holds the time.
Sanskrit sounds for readers. Today, the map: consonants in rows from throat to palate to roof to teeth to lips, and c always said ch.
Your line: Sanskrit sounds for readers, the alphabet in sound. Today, catch one word you say often and ask where in the mouth its first sound lives. Day one thousand forty-two.

howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit recite the consonants row by row, ka-kha-ga-gha-nga and onward, learning each row by where the mouth makes it, from the throat to the lips.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: ka, the first consonant, made in the throat, with the short a inside it.

trapdoor: what you thought: the alphabet is a list to memorize.
what it means: it's a map of the mouth, row by row from the throat to the lips.
what a scholar hears: the varga order, velar, palatal, retroflex, dental, labial, each row closing in a nasal.
